FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 1 of 18  BRIEF STATEMENT OF REASONS FOR DECISION:
1.
The accused in present case has been sent for trial for the offence punishable under Section 406 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code (Act 45 of 1960) (hereinafter referred the 'IPC').
2. Brief facts of the case, as per prosecution, are that the instant FIR was registered on the complaint of one Snehalata, a resident of Metro View Apartment.

The complainant has alleged that the accused represented herself to be a financially sound person to her and her other friends namely Anita and State vs Bijender Kaur on 19 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/104817368/
1 Reena, and thereby induced them to become a member of the committee and deliver to her an amount of Rs.2,25,000 (from the complainant), Rs.1,90,625/- (from Anita) and Rs.85,070/- (from Reena) on various dates and later when they demanded the money of the committee she refused to return the said amount to them and also abruptly closed the committee, thereby committed the offence under Section 420 IPC.

Furthermore, it was also alleged against the complainant that she was entrusted the aforesaid amount by the complainant and her friends but dishonestly misappropriated and used it for her own use and thereby committed the offence under Section 406 IPC.
3.
On the basis of the abovementioned complaint, the present FIR got registered upon the directions of the Ld. Predecessor of this Court.
Investigation got started.
During the investigation the statements of the complainant and other co-complainants were recorded, the accused was joined in the investigation.

After investigation, the final report under Section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred the 'CrPC') against accused Bijender Kaur for the offences punishable under Sections 406/420 IPC was filed.

The cognizance of the offence under Section 406/420 IPC was taken by Ld. Predecessor of this Court and was admitted to bail by the Court.

After compliance of the provisions of Section 207 CrPC,
charge for the offence under Section 420/406 IPC was framed against the accused to which the accused had pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. The prosecution has examined 5 witnesses in support of its case.
6. PW-1 Smt. Snehlata Devi is a public witness and the complainant of this case.
She deposed that she used to reside in the same society as that of the accused, where the accused used to run a boutique.
She further deposed that the accused induced her by presenting herself to be financially strong and rich.
She further deposed that the accused asked her to become a member of a committee which was being run by her in the year 2012 which she joined and kept on making timely payments till April, 2013.
She further deposed that she made a total payment of Rs. 2,25,000/- to the accused and thereafter the accused abruptly closed the committee stating that it had gone into a loss.
She further deposed that upon being requested by her to return the amount the accused refused to return the same.
She further deposed that thereafter, she took steps for registration of FIR and the same was registered upon the directions of the Ld. Predecessor Court.

She further deposed that before the registration of FIR the accused also gave her a cheque of Rs. 4.5 lakhs of her husband but she wrote 'for security purposes only' but the same also got dishonoured.
She further deposed that the diary entry of the accused qua her part payment was also made in exhibit Ex. PW-1/E.

She further deposed that her friend Anita also used to run a committee with the accused and she used to handover the FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 3 of 18 amount of the committee to the PW-1 and she used to handover the same to the accused.
She lastly deposed in examination in chief that her friend Anita was also cheated by the accused for an amount of Rs. 1,90,625/-.

10. The witnesses were duly cross
- examined by Ld. counsel for the accused.
Thereafter, on the submissions of Ld. APP for the State, PE was closed.
The statement of the accused under Section 313 CrPC, after putting entire incriminating evidence against her, was recorded.

The accused has denied commission of the offence and has stated that she had been falsely implicated in the present case by the complainant as a counter blast to the dismissal of her case against the deceased husband of the accused.
The accused examined herself in defence evidence and, thereafter, the matter was fixed for final arguments.
11. Sh. Rohit Grewal, Ld. APP for State would argue that the prosecution has proved its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.
Hence, it is prayed, the accused may be convicted for the offences.
12. On the other hand, it is submitted by Sh. Vikram Panwar, Ld. Advocate for the accused, that the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.
There is no evidence against the accused on record to show that she had committed the criminal breach of trust or cheating against anyone.
Hence, it is prayed that the accused may be acquitted.
13. I have heard the submissions on behalf of both the parties and carefully perused the material available on record.

4 14. It is a settled proposition of criminal law that the prosecution is supposed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt by leading reliable, cogent and convincing evidence.
The primary burden of proof for proving the offences in a criminal trial rests on the shoulders of the prosecution.
Further, an accused is entitled to benefit of every reasonable doubt appearing qua the material facts.
15. The accused herein has been facing the trial for the offences punishable under Section 406 and Section 420, of the IPC.
Before, proceeding any further, it would be appropriate to discuss the law relating to these offences.
16. Section 406 IPC provides punishment for criminal breach of trust.

The law provides that a person being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property,
dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use the said property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or willfully suffers any other person so to do, commits criminal breach of trust.
17. Section 420 IPC provides punishment for cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.

In order to constitute, offence under Section 420 IPC, the prosecution has to establish that the accused had deceived the complainant/victim dishonestly inducing him to part with any property in his favour which he would not have parted but for the deception played on him.

Thus, the essential ingredients of the offence is that there must be dishonest intention on the part of the accused at the time FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 8 of 18 of making the representation to the complainant / victim on the basis which the complainant / victim part with his property.
Intention must be dishonest and there must also be mens rea.
Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Samir Sahay v. State of U.P., (2018) 14 SCC 233 has discussed the ingredients and the law related to the offence of cheating under Section 415 and 420, of the IPC.

It has been held as under:
"6.Before we proceed further to examine the contentions of the learned counsel for the parties, it is necessary to notice the ingredients for establishing a charge under Section 420 IPC. Section 415 IPC defines "cheating" which is to the following effect:
"415.Cheating.-Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property
, is said to "cheat".

17. Section 420 IPC is with regard to the cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property which is to the following effect: "420.Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.-Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 9 of 18 whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and State vs Bijender Kaur on 19 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/104817368/
5 which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine."
"18.
According to Section 420 IPC, the inducement must be fraudulent and dishonest which depends upon the intention of the accused at the time of inducement.
This Court had occasion to consider Section 420 IPC in Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar [Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar, (2000) 4 SCC 168 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 786] .

sentences.text: This Court after noticing the provisions of Section 415 and 420 IPC stated the following in paras 14 and 15 : (SCC pp. 176-77) "14.
On a reading of the section it is manifest that in the definition there are set forth two separate classes of acts which the person deceived may be induced to do.
In the first place he may be induced fraudulently or dishonestly to deliver any property to any person.
The second class of acts set forth in the section is the doing or omitting to do anything which the person deceived would not do or omit to do if he were not so deceived.
In the first class of cases the inducing must be fraudulent or dishonest.
In the second class of acts, the inducing must be intentional but not fraudulent or dishonest.
FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 10 of 18 "15
. In determining the question it has to be kept in mind that the distinction between mere breach of contract and the offence of cheating is a fine one.
It depends upon the intention of the accused at the time of inducement which may be judged by his subsequent conduct but for this subsequent conduct is not the sole test.

Mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction, that is the time when the offence is said to have been committed.
Therefore it is the intention which is the gist of the offence.
To hold a person guilty of cheating it is necessary to show that he had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise.
From his mere failure to keep up promise subsequently such a culpable intention right at the beginning, that is, when he made the promise cannot be presumed."
"19. Again in Dalip Kaur v. Jagnar Singh [Dalip Kaur v. Jagnar Singh, (2009) 14 SCC 696 : (2010) 2 SCC (Cri) 223] , this Court noticed the ingredients of Section 420 IPC.

If the dispute between the parties was essentially a civil dispute resulting from a breach of contract on the part of the appellants by non-refunding the amount of advance the same would not constitute an offence of cheating.
Similar is the legal position in respect of an offence of criminal breach of trust having regard to its definition contained in Section 405 of the Penal Code.

sentences.text: As mentioned above, Section 415 has two parts.

While in the first part, the person must "dishonestly" or "fraudulently" induce the complainant to deliver any property; in the second part,
the person should intentionally induce the complainant to do or omit to do a thing.
That is to say, in the first part, inducement must be dishonest or fraudulent.
In the second part, the inducement should be intentional.

As observed by this FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 13 of 18 Court in Jaswantrai Manilal Akhaney v. State of Bombay [Jaswantrai Manilal Akhaney v. State of Bombay, AIR 1956 SC 575 : 1956 Cri LJ 1116], a guilty intention is an essential ingredient of the offence of cheating.

18. In view of the above discussed legal position, I shall proceed to decide the present matter.
FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 15 of 18 19

. It has been alleged in the complaint that the accused had taken amount from the complainant and the other co-complainants in the name of the committee and thereafter refused to return the promised amount or even the principal amount.
However, she did not return those amounts to the complainants.
Later on, it came to the knowledge of the complainants that the accused had used the said money for her use and misappropriated the same.
20. The complainant had appeared in evidence to prove the contentions made by her in her complaint.
However, what needs to be appreciated that even though the entire case is based upon her complaint, it has nowhere been shown by her as to how she had transferred the said amount to the accused.
Furthermore, none of the complainant witnesses were able to bring any receipt to show that they had handed over the said alleged amount to the accused.

21. Furthermore, another aspect which needs to be appreciated is that the alleged diary of the accused Ex. PW-1/E was never sent by the IO to the FSL for examination and identifying her handwriting for the reasons best known to him.

State vs Bijender Kaur on 19 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/104817368/
8 22.

For the purposes of both the offences with which the accused has been charged with, it needs to be shown in the first place that the amounts were transferred by the complainants to her in the name of the alleged committee.
However, as discussed above no receipt or bank transactions has been shown by the complainant showing any such transfer or handling over the money to the accused by them.

It also begets reasoning that any educated individual would give such high amount to FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 16 of 18 another individual only on the basis of mutual understanding and without any documentary proof or receipt issued in their name.
23.
In light of the above, it has remained not proved beyond reasonable doubts that the accused had taken any money from the complainant as stated by her in the complaint.

Further, even if it is presumed, for the sake of the arguments, that the accused had taken the said amount from the complainant for the purpose of the committee, there is nothing on record to show as to the existence of any dishonest intention of the accused at the very time of taking the money.

24. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 during their cross-examinations, have stated that they did not have the copy of the committee documents or receipts issued by the accused which contained the details of the transactions.
There is nothing on record to show the details of the transactions.
Therefore, it cannot be said for sure that the complainants had actually given any amount to the accused.
25. Further, in the complaint, it is stated by PW-2 Anita that she used to handover the amount to the PW-1/complainant and she in turn used to hand over the same to the accused.
Thus, even as per the PW-2, the amounts were never handed over to the accused directly.
No liability of the accused can be fixed on the basis of the averment that the amount was handed over to the complainant by her.

Furthermore, the complainants have not even deposed in their examinations that the accused had an intention to defraud or cheat them from the very beginning, thus no intent to cheat at the time of inducement was shown to have ever existed by the prosecution.
FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 17 of 18 26.
In view of the discussion herein-above, I am of the considered opinion that it can be safely held that the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.
It has remained not proved that the complainant had provided the aforesaid amount to the accused in the very first place.
It has also remained not proved that the complainant had asked the accused to return the amount.
The burden was on the prosecution to prove the ingredients of the offence punishable u/s 406 or Section 420 IPC against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.
However, it has failed to discharge the burden.

Hence, the accused is acquitted for the offence under Section 420/ 406 IPC.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
4 14. It is a settled proposition of criminal law that the prosecution is supposed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt by leading reliable, cogent and convincing evidence.
The primary burden of proof for proving the offences in a criminal trial rests on the shoulders of the prosecution.
Further, an accused is entitled to benefit of every reasonable doubt appearing qua the material facts.
Thus, the essential ingredients of the offence is that there must be dishonest intention on the part of the accused at the time FIR No.481/2016 State Vs. Bijender Kaur Page no. 8 of 18 of making the representation to the complainant / victim on the basis which the complainant / victim part with his property.
Intention must be dishonest and there must also be mens rea.
Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Samir Sahay v. State of U.P., (2018) 14 SCC 233 has discussed the ingredients and the law related to the offence of cheating under Section 415 and 420, of the IPC.
This Court had occasion to consider Section 420 IPC in Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar [Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar, (2000) 4 SCC 168 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 786] .
"19. Again in Dalip Kaur v. Jagnar Singh [Dalip Kaur v. Jagnar Singh, (2009) 14 SCC 696 : (2010) 2 SCC (Cri) 223] , this Court noticed the ingredients of Section 420 IPC.
If the dispute between the parties was essentially a civil dispute resulting from a breach of contract on the part of the appellants by non-refunding the amount of advance the same would not constitute an offence of cheating.

. It has been alleged in the complaint that the accused had taken amount from the complainant and the other co-complainants in the name of the committee and thereafter refused to return the promised amount or even the principal amount.
However, she did not return those amounts to the complainants.
Later on, it came to the knowledge of the complainants that the accused had used the said money for her use and misappropriated the same.
20. The complainant had appeared in evidence to prove the contentions made by her in her complaint.
However, what needs to be appreciated that even though the entire case is based upon her complaint, it has nowhere been shown by her as to how she had transferred the said amount to the accused.
Furthermore, none of the complainant witnesses were able to bring any receipt to show that they had handed over the said alleged amount to the accused.
For the purposes of both the offences with which the accused has been charged with, it needs to be shown in the first place that the amounts were transferred by the complainants to her in the name of the alleged committee.
Furthermore, the complainants have not even deposed in their examinations that the accused had an intention to defraud or cheat them from the very beginning, thus no intent to cheat at the time of inducement was shown to have ever existed by the prosecution.
In view of the discussion herein-above, I am of the considered opinion that it can be safely held that the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.
It has remained not proved that the complainant had provided the aforesaid amount to the accused in the very first place.
It has also remained not proved that the complainant had asked the accused to return the amount.
The burden was on the prosecution to prove the ingredients of the offence punishable u/s 406 or Section 420 IPC against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.
However, it has failed to discharge the burden.
